newsitem.title: UK: UK chemical industry says output rise not steady.
newsitem.headline: UK chemical industry says output rise not steady.

text.p: Britain's chemical industry said on Thursday that the upward trend in sales and output volumes was "not very steady."
However, the Chemical Industries Association (CIA) said in the April edition of its Economics Bulletin that smaller companies, particularly those in contract manufacturing, "remain busy."

The CIA also said there were "encouraging signs of strengthening in the polymer market, where it is felt that improved demand is now feeding straight through to production and is no longer being distorted by inventory movements."
The CIA said there was concern about the strength of sterling, which was affecting profit margins in the short term and was likely to "be reflected in reduced export volumes as the year progresses."

The organisation forecast in January that UK chemicals output would rise by three percent in 1996, with exports climbing by five percent, but it said these forecasts "may need to be adjusted downwards" if the pound's current strength was maintained.

It said UK chemicals output in 1996 rose by 2.0 percent, compared with a rise of 1.4 percent for the OECD economies as a whole. The CIA said the British performance was "sustained by export sales, while home sales actually fell in the second half of the year."
Exports rose by 4.8 percent last year to 22.2 billion stg, producing a favourable trade balance of 3.9 billion stg compared with 3.3 billion in 1995.
The CIA said production of basic chemcials was flat last year, balanced by stronger performances from paints, toiletries and fibres.
